query: Starting from bulk HfNbTaTiZr, whose low thermal conductivity is desirable for thermal insulation, what single intervention could further reduce its phonon thermal conductivity relative to the starting material? The hypothesis should address the limitation that phonon and electronic contributions are estimated to be similar from nearly 0 to 200 K, while the available 300–1200 K measurements concern a sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen. Specify the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the unchanged bulk baseline, the temperatures and material states for which the prediction applies, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing porosity into the HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy can further reduce its phonon thermal conductivity.
generation.mechanism: derived from materials-science principles, based on the similar lattice distortion effect and phonon scattering mechanisms in high-entropy alloys
generation.uncertainty: limited by the availability of experimental data on the thermal conductivity of porous HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy

falsification_experiment.design: measure the thermal conductivity of porous HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy and compare it to the bulk material
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the thermal conductivity of the porous material is not lower than the bulk material, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The unique properties of the porous HECs are ascribed to the high-entropy effects and dual-porosity structures. The severe lattice distortions in the HECs lead to the low intrinsic thermal conductivity by reducing phonons’ mean free path and increasing phonon scattering. Moreover, this results in high compressive strength by inhibiting the crack generations and propagations. The dual-porosity structure possesses several small pores in high-porosity ceramics. These small pores are more efficient in scattering phonon thermal conductivity and inhibiting crack propagations, which are beneficial to improving the thermal insulation and mechanical properties of the porous HECs.

We applied atomic-resolution chemical mapping for the distribution and fluctuation of elements in high-entropy thermoelectric materials with a variety of elemental combinations. With the fluctuation evaluation of each element, we clearly revealed that the fluctuations of alloying elements were directly related to the discrepancy on atomic mass, radius, and electronegativity of these elements to the matrix elements in high-entropy samples. With the estimation on the respective contributions of the element characteristics, we found that the mass and electronegativity have the comparable contribution to local chemical fluctuation while there is a slight influence from the radius. Moreover, the local chemical fluctuation tailored by altering the constituent elements could reduce the lattice thermal conductivity, in addition to the increased entropy by combining more elements. Large lattice distortion and strain fluctuation were induced by strong elemental fluctuation to largely strengthen phonon scattering for low lattice thermal conductivity. As the outputs of MD simulation are mainly atomic trajectories, the thermal conductivity discussed in this paper is the lattice thermal conductivity. The effects of chemical composition in terms of content of the constituent atoms, size of the HEA and temperature on the lattice thermal conductivity of the CoCrFeNiCu HEA are investigated.

In order to address the thermal properties, we investigated the temperature dependent Seebeck coefficient S(T) and thermal conductivity κ(T). The Seebeck coefficient (Fig. 4a) is nearly temperature independent and exhibits small values across the entire temperature range. This indicates typical metallic behavior, similar to what is seen in other HEAs such as YxCoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi, and (BiSbTe1.5Se1.5)1-xAgx. This supports our conclusion that the uranium f-states are delocalized and thus do not significantly impact the electrical transport behavior. At lower temperatures, S(T) exhibits a weak peak around 50 K, which we propose is due to phonon drag effect, as is seen in other HEAs due to plastic deformation at high strain rates. The thermal conductivity (Fig. 4b) next suggests that phonon scattering mechanisms dominate the thermal transport, as would be anticipated based on the disordered arrangement of atoms on the lattice.
